inline.s: The dream of ignorance is a great dream, like a virtual world in which countless dreamers exist and can interact with one another, and can build and destroy their surroundings and the objects in them. Yet people find it hard to believe that they are in the dream of ignorance and that everything is an illusion. This is not strange: if you have never awakened, how could you know you are dreaming? Nevertheless, through the ages countless men who have clearly seen the mind and realized their nature have all confirmed that we are in the dream of ignorance. Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way (Zhengdao Ge) says:
“In the dream the six realms plainly show; once wakened, all the vast world is empty and hollow.”
By practicing ourselves, we too can confirm this, and that is the repeatability of science.

[Reference] There is at present a view in the scientific community that the universe is a virtual world with an extremely intricate program. That program follows two basic principles (the rules of the game):

1. The principle of mental guidance. The moment the heart of the player moves, the system of this virtual world activates for him; when the player's heart remains still and unmoved, without even the subtlest thought, the system of this virtual world closes for him of itself. This is what is meant by all dharmas being mind-only: when the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease.

2. The principle of dynamic revision. In accord with what the player's avatar does in the virtual world, the system constantly revises and corrects his fate data, and by this determines his present condition and his future. If he has done good, his fate turns toward the good; if he has done evil, his fate turns toward the evil. Fate is always what one makes for oneself and receives of oneself — this is karmic retribution.
A dream, if you take it as real, will enslave you. Master Taixu said:
The mind within the dream
, that is the mind of the ordinary man;
the mind that knows it is dreaming within the dream
, that is the mind of the bodhisattva;
the mind that awakens
(waking from the dream)
, that is the mind of the Buddha.”
(from the Outline of the Vijñaptimātratā View)
The Compendium of Mahāyāna Meanings (Dasheng Yizhang) says:

“Buddha is named for his virtue. Buddha means awareness and knowing, and from this the title is established. Awareness has two meanings. The first is called awareness-as-detection, as when a man detects a thief. The second is called awareness-as-awakening, as when a man wakes from sleep
(waking from sleep)

. Awareness-of-detection is set against the affliction obstacle; the harm wrought by afflictions is like a thief's, and only the sage's awareness knows not to be harmed by them, hence it is called awareness. The Nirvana Sutra says: ‘As a man detects a thief and the thief can do nothing, so also is the Buddha.’ The awareness of awakening is set against the cognitive obstacle; the dark drowse of ignorance is like sleep, and when the sage's wisdom rises and there is suddenly great enlightenment,
as one wakes from sleep
(waking from a dream)

, hence it is called awareness. Being able to awaken oneself and also to awaken others, with awakening practice brought to its utmost fulfillment, is why it is called Buddha. To say he awakens himself sets him apart from ordinary men; to say he awakens others distinguishes him from the Two Vehicles; awakening practice brought to full consummation shows his difference from the bodhisattvas.”

[Affliction obstacle] Because ordinary people do not know the emptiness of self and cling to a self, and from that self spring greed, anger, delusion, and other afflictions, they thereby obstruct the manifestation of nirvana; hence it is called an obstacle. [Knowledge obstacle] This is the cognitive obstacle. Because ordinary people do not know the emptiness of dharmas and cling to the various dharmas, they produce all sorts of erroneous knowledge that obstructs the arising of bodhi; hence it is called an obstacle. The sutra says: ‘If the attachment to dharmas is not removed, the cognitive obstacle arises and blocks bodhi.’
Therefore the practice should be pursued on two fronts: first, detection — to know the thought the instant it arises; second, awakening — no longer clinging to appearances.
Q: The Chan masters speak of ‘a dream within a dream.’ What does this mean?

Answer: The dream of ignorance is the first occurrence of the word ‘dream.’ The self-nature is the dreamer within the dream of ignorance, and because the self-nature deludedly clings to the physical body as itself and takes the shadows of the six sense-objects for its own mind, there therefore arise birth and death (birth-and-death in segments) and the cycle of rebirth — this is the second occurrence of the word ‘dream,’ the carrying on of the dream of rebirth within the dream of ignorance, which the ancients called ‘a dream within a dream.’ The five aggregates, body, and mind are the dreamers of the dream of rebirth. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
‘All beings, from beginnings beginning, are in all manner of upside-down confusion, like a lost man who takes the four directions to be in different places
(for example, taking east for west and south for north)

, and deludedly revere the four great elements as the form of a self and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the form of the self-mind. It is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in empty space
(flowers)
and a second moon. … From this false construction they turn about in birth and death.’
(For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

[Five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volition, and the aggregate of consciousness — these five arise by accumulation, and so are called the ‘five aggregates’; and because they can cover over man's true nature, confusing and overturning him and driving him to create all manner of karma, they are also called the ‘five shrouds’ (five yin). Of these, the aggregate of form refers to matter, and is called ‘dharmas of form’; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness belong to the mental, and are called ‘dharmas of mind.’ These are the five great constituents of body and mind, of which the aggregate of form is the physical body while the other four (feeling, perception, volition, consciousness) are mind. [Four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth is hard in nature, water moist, fire warm, and wind moving. All the tangible things of the world possess these four natures — hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion — and so are called ‘great.’ [Shadows of the six sense-objects] The various imaginings produced when the six faculties meet the six sense-objects; because these imaginings are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantom images of the six sense-objects.

When afflictions are completely cut off, one ends the birth-and-death of segments and leaves the dream of rebirth; when ignorance is completely cut off, one ends the birth-and-death of transformation and leaves the dream of ignorance.

[Birth-and-death in segments] Beings within the three realms and six destinies, owing to the good and evil karma they have created, have lifespans with fixed limits and bodies with fixed forms, and so their birth and death is called ‘birth-and-death in segments.’ One who ends birth-and-death in segments escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Birth-and-death of transformation] The sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended birth-and-death in segments. In the course of their practice, deluded imaginings gradually vanish while realization gradually grows; this passage from delusion to awakening differs in every stage, and the moving from an earlier stage into a later one is precisely like a birth-and-death, whose transformations are subtle and unfathomable beyond all thought — hence it is called ‘birth-and-death of transformation.’ One who ends birth-and-death of transformation perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Q: How does one leave the dream of rebirth?
Answer:

To leave this dream of rebirth, this endless round of birth and death, one must achieve it through practice. The common path is to cut off afflictions completely, so that at the moment of death one can be the master; then one can end birth and death and leave the cycle. The patriarch Huangbo says:
‘When a person is about to die, he should only contemplate that the five aggregates
(form, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness)

are all empty, that the four great elements have no self, that the true mind has no form and comes not nor goes. At birth the nature comes not; at death the nature goes not. Serenely one passes into serene nirvana, mind and realm as one. If one can but understand this at once and at that very place, and be no longer bound by the three times, then one is a person who has left the world.’
(from the Essentials of the Transmission of Mind) If one cultivates the Pure Land path, one needs only sustain ten recitations at death (see details in
The Conditions for Rebirth
), and touch the response of Amitabha Buddha's coming to receive and guide one, then one leaves the dream of rebirth and is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Q: It is said above that ‘all dharmas are illusions.’ Does that mean the ālaya-vijñāna is also an illusion?
Answer: Yes, the ālaya-vijñāna is an illusion. Because this question has long been a matter of considerable dispute, let me add a few citations here:
In the Vimalakīrti Sutra (Shuo Wugoucheng Jing), volume six, it speaks of ‘non-ālaya,’ and the Buddha says:
‘Though he delights in contemplating
non-ālaya
, he does not cast away the treasury of pure dharmas; though he contemplates that all dharmas are ultimately unborn, he still bears the burden of benefiting sentient beings.’
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, volume 576, it also speaks of ‘non-ālaya,’ and Mañjuśrī (the bodhisattva of wondrous auspiciousness) says:

‘All sentient beings may be established in the Buddha's wondrous Dharma, in the awakening of wisdom that is unmoved, knowing the nature of dharmas to be empty — without name and without form, without support and without abiding, without grasping and without attachment, without obstruction and without clinging, like empty space,
non-ālaya

, and non-niyanta; the supreme still, the utmost still; unborn and unceasing, undefiled and immaculate, uncompleted and undestroyed, neither existing nor non-existent. Thereby one attains in it the profound patience (kṣānti) and is never far from the Buddha's wondrous Dharma.’
[Niyanta] A different name for greed, meaning the utmost insatiable craving that knows no end.
The scriptural passages above all state that the ālaya-vijñāna is not real, but is an illusion.

In his Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu groups all dharmas into five great categories: dharmas of mind, dharmas of mind-mental factors, dharmas not associated with mind, and unconditioned dharmas. The ālaya-vijñāna belongs to the category of mind-dharmas among all dharmas. The Buddha says:
‘All dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame.’
(from the Small Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, volume ten) And the Buddha says:
‘Know that all dharmas are empty, like an illusion without reality, having no root.’

(from the Sutra of the Keeper of the World, the eighteenth, chapter on the nature of dharmas, third.) Since all dharmas are like an illusion without reality, and the ālaya-vijñāna is one dharma among all dharmas, it is of course like an illusion without reality.
Q: Why, in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, does the Buddha say:
‘The true self that the Tathāgata speaks of today is called the Buddha-nature.’
Answer: The ‘true self’ spoken of here is relative to the false self of the five aggregates, body, and mind. In the Tenth Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching, the Sixth Patriarch says:
‘Only recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, unmoving and still, unborn and unceasing.’
And the meaning of ‘unborn and unceasing’ is that originally there were none, exactly as the Sixth Patriarch explains ‘unborn and unceasing’ in the Ninth Chapter on the Dharma of Protection:
‘Originally there was no birth, and now there is no ceasing.’
In the Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury, the Buddha says:
‘All dharmas are unborn and unceasing, without form, without activity.’
This shows that the original nature (namely, the tathāgatagarbha, the Buddha-nature) is also an illusion.
Q: If this is so, is the dharmakāya itself also an illusion?
Answer: The Mahāyāna Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground (Xin Di Guan Jing) says:
‘Always contemplate the Buddha's wondrous dharmakāya, whose essence and nature are like empty space, ungraspable.’
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says:
‘The dharmakāya is like an illusion or a dream — how can it be praised? Knowing the nature to be without self-nature and unborn, that is what is called praising the Buddha.’
Q: Then who is bound? Who creates karma? Who transmigrates? Who is liberated? And to where is one liberated?

Answer: The self-nature is bound; the self-nature creates karma; the self-nature transmigrates; the self-nature is liberated. Liberation has two stages: if one ends birth-and-death in segments, one leaves the cycle and escapes the three realms; if one ends birth-and-death of transformation, one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. As for where one is liberated, according to the levels of liberation there are four lands where one may dwell: the land where ordinary men and sages dwell together, the land of expedient remainder, the land of real reward and adornment, and the land of eternal stillness and light. The land where ordinary men and sages dwell together is the land inhabited by ordinary men together with sages who manifest bodies and preach the Dharma for the sake of teaching sentient beings; the land of expedient remainder is the land of the Two Vehicles and of bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the dharmakāya; the land of real reward and adornment is the land of the Buddha's reward-body and of the bodhisattvas on the grounds; the land of eternal stillness and light is the land where the Buddha's pure dharmakāya manifests quiescence. All four lands are doings within the dream of ignorance. A self-nature of a higher level may go to a lower land, but a self-nature of a lower level cannot go to a higher land. After attaining Buddhahood, one may either remain in the dream of ignorance to teach and save sentient beings, or enter extinction, whereupon that dreamer no longer dreams the dream of ignorance. (For a fuller account of the self-nature, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
Q: The saying ‘Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor things’ — what does it mean?
Answer:
The Compendium of the Five Lamps records:
A monk asked, ‘Why does the Master say
mind is Buddha
?’ The Master
(Mazu)
said, ‘To stop the infant's crying
(this is an expedient saying for those just beginning to study)
.’ The monk said, ‘When the crying stops, how then?’ The Master said, ‘
not mind, not Buddha
.’ The monk said, ‘Apart from these two kinds of people, how do you instruct them?’ The Master said, ‘Say to him
(him)
say
not a thing
